power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text:  These findings provide important insight into factors associated with knowledge of ticks, tick-borne diseases and engagement in protective behaviours in an English sample, an underexplored research area to date.
 Public knowledge related to ticks is incomplete, with several psychological variables associated with knowledge of ticks, tick-borne diseases and engagement in protective behaviours.
 These findings can be used to support future work focused on public health intervention design and evaluation in the context of ticks and tick-borne diseases.
Ticks and the diseases that they can carry pose a risk to public health.

Pathogens transmitted by ticks were responsible for most vector borne diseases in North America, Europe and Asia between 2004 and 2016, with Lyme disease (LD) being the most prevalent tick-borne disease (TBD) in the northern hemisphere [1, 2].
text.formatted: Pathogens transmitted by ticks were responsible for most vector borne diseases in North America, Europe and Asia between 2004 and 2016, with Lyme disease (LD) being the most prevalent tick-borne disease (TBD) in the northern hemisphere <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: Engagement in protective actions such as performing tick checks or wearing protective clothing can reduce the risk of being bitten by ticks (and subsequently reduce the risk of disease).

Although the recommended protective actions to prevent tick bites are relatively simple to enact and require little specialist equipment (e.g., wearing long sleeved shirts and long trousers, avoiding walking through long grass, wearing insect repellent) [4, 5], individual engagement in protective behaviours can vary.
text.formatted: Although the recommended protective actions to prevent tick bites are relatively simple to enact and require little specialist equipment (e.g., wearing long sleeved shirts and long trousers, avoiding walking through long grass, wearing insect repellent) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>, individual engagement in protective behaviours can vary.

text.text: Metaanalytic work [6] has indicated that both environmental and behavioural factors contribute to the risk of being bitten by ticks.
text.formatted: Metaanalytic work <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> has indicated that both environmental and behavioural factors contribute to the risk of being bitten by ticks.

text.text: However, a 2014 UK survey found that 20% of participants always performed tick checks following rambling or walking, with 52% of the sample stating that they never performed checks [7].
text.formatted: However, a 2014 UK survey found that 20% of participants always performed tick checks following rambling or walking, with 52% of the sample stating that they never performed checks <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Although evidence can be inconsistent in relation to the effectiveness of these behaviours in the prevention of disease [8], exploring the factors that can predict engagement with protective behaviours provides important insight and potential targets for behavioural interventions to support engagement with protective behaviours.
text.formatted: Although evidence can be inconsistent in relation to the effectiveness of these behaviours in the prevention of disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>, exploring the factors that can predict engagement with protective behaviours provides important insight and potential targets for behavioural interventions to support engagement with protective behaviours.

text.text: While behaviour is multi-faceted and unlikely to depend on one factor alone, knowledge and awareness of protective behaviours to engage in (and the risks associated with ticks) is likely to play an important role in shaping risk perceptions and behavioural intentions.

Previous research from Sweden demonstrated that higher knowledge about ticks, TBDs and protective actions were positively associated with performing tick checks, wearing repellent and wearing protective clothing [9].
text.formatted: Previous research from Sweden demonstrated that higher knowledge about ticks, TBDs and protective actions were positively associated with performing tick checks, wearing repellent and wearing protective clothing <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: While assessing levels of knowledge related to ticks in the general population can provide important insights to support the development of public health messaging and interventions, identifying the factors that are associated with knowledge can provide further evidence to support the tailoring and targeting of interventions, an area that is underexplored within population samples from England.

The aim of the present study was to identify the sociodemographic and psychological factors associated with knowledge of ticks and engagement with protective behaviours in a sample of adults from England.
An online cross-sectional survey was conducted by Ipsos, a market research consultancy company.
The survey formed part of the Public Perceptions Tracker (PPT), a quarterly survey commissioned by UKHSA.
Data were collected between the 20 th and 30 th May 2025 (wave 31).
One thousand four hundred participants completed the survey.
To be eligible, respondents had to be aged over 18 and resident in England at the time of survey completion.

Participants who stated that they had never heard of ticks (n=296) were excluded, as it was unlikely that they would give valid/reliable answers to tick-related questions, resulting in a final sample of 1,104 participants.

The largest number of participants were aged between 25-34 (20.93%). 653 participants identified as female (59.15%), 449 as male (40.67%) and 2 as other (prefer to describe/prefer not to say) (0.18%).
For this study, only questions about ticks, TBDs and sociodemographic characteristics were included in the analysis.
Participants were given the option to skip questions that included images of ticks.
Questions focused on knowledge, attitudes and beliefs related to ticks, TBDs and engagement in protective behaviours.
Sociodemographic factors included gender identity, age, ethnicity, UK region and urban/rural classification of residence.

Psychological factors included risk perceptions, previous experience of bites, selfefficacy (belief of an individual in their ability to enact a behaviour), response-efficacy (belief that an action will prevent or mitigate a hazard), social norms, seeing/hearing information about protection from tick bites and actions to take following a bite, and self-reported knowledge.

Knowledge of ticks and TBDs (herein referred to as knowledge) was calculated by totalling the number of correctly selected responses to questions on knowledge of ticks (n=7) in addition to the number of incorrect responses not selected.
This ensured that participants would not receive high scores by selecting all available response options.
Responses of 'don't know/not sure' were treated as 'incorrect' (coded as 0).
The maximum possible score was 35, with higher scores indicating higher knowledge.

Engagement in protective behaviours (herein referred to as behaviour) was calculated by totalling the number of actions selected in response to the question 'Which, if any, of the following have you done in the past few months to prevent tick bites or catching diseases from ticks'.
The maximum possible score was 8, with higher scores indicating a higher number of completed behaviours.
Eighty-six participants (7.79%) skipped questions related to ticks when the opportunity was provided.
These data were treating as missing in analyses.
Separate multiple linear regression models were fitted, one for each outcome (n=2).
All sociodemographic and psychological variables were included simultaneously within each model.
For the behaviours outcome, knowledge of ticks and TBDs was also included as a predictor.
Only participants who reported spending time in outdoor spaces within the previous three months were included in the behaviours analysis (n=888).
Due to a relatively large number of 'don't know' responses, most predictor variables were analysed categorically, with a separate group for 'don't know' responses to minimise missing data.
Reference categories for each predictor are presented in table 1.
text.formatted: Reference categories for each predictor are presented in table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: As a result, we specified a conservative significance threshold (p<.001) a-priori to control for the risk of Type 1 error arising from multiple comparisons.
text.formatted: As a result, we specified a conservative significance threshold (p<.001) a-priori to control for the risk of Type 1 error arising from multiple comparisons.

text.text: Results that met this criterion are marked in the tables below with ***.
All analyses were performed in R (version 4.3.1).
The average score for knowledge was 20 (57.14%, SD=6.25), and the average number of behaviours engaged in was 1.43 (17.88%, SD=1.17).
A large number of participants provided 'don't know' responses to questions, with only 419 participants (37.95%) not providing any 'don't know' responses across questions.
Descriptive statistics for individual survey items are provided in the supplementary materials.
Participants who perceived tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) as not serious had significant negative associations for knowledge compared to those who perceived TBE as serious.

Self-efficacy was also a significant predictor of knowledge, where participants who responded with 'don't know' for knowing how to check for ticks or for being confident in removing a tick had significant negative associations for knowledge compared to those who agreed they knew how to, or were confident in removal.
There was also a significant negative association for knowing how to check for ticks for neutral or disagree responses compared to agree responses.

Participants who self-reported knowing not much or nothing about Lyme disease had significant negative associations for knowledge compared to participants who reported great or fair levels of knowledge.

Participants who responded with 'don't know' when asked about how much they agreed with the statement 'being bitten depends on my actions' had significant negative associations for knowledge compared to participants with agree responses.

Participants who responded with a neutral or disagree response to the question 'I would normally forget to check for ticks' had significant negative associations for knowledge compared to participants who responded with agree.

text.text: Participants who were from Black ethnic backgrounds had significant positive associations for behaviours compared to participants from white ethnic backgrounds.

Participants who reported seeing not much or no information related to protection from tick bites had significant negative associations for behaviours compared to those who reported seeing a little or a lot of information.

Compared to those who thought they had been bitten by a tick (but were not sure), those who had never been bitten by a tick or responded with 'don't know' had significant negative associations for behaviours (b=-0.82, p<.001 and b=-0.85, p<.001 respectively).
text.formatted: Compared to those who thought they had been bitten by a tick (but were not sure), those who had never been bitten by a tick or responded with 'don't know' had significant negative associations for behaviours (b=-0.82, p<.001 and b=-0.85, p<.001 respectively).

text.text: Participants who provided neutral or disagree responses to the question 'I don't think about ticks' had significant positive associations for behaviours compared to those who provided agree responses.
There was also a significant positive association between knowledge of ticks and TBDs and behaviours.
The aim of the present study was to identify the factors associated with knowledge of ticks and TBDs and engagement with protective behaviours in a sample of adults from England.
The results revealed that perceived severity of disease, self-efficacy, social norms and self-reported knowledge were associated with knowledge related to ticks.

For engagement with protective behaviours, having suspected tick experience, belonging to a black ethnic group, having seen or heard information about ticks, higher knowledge of ticks were all associated.
With the exception of ethnicity, no other sociodemographic factors were associated with behaviours, and no sociodemographic factors were associated with knowledge.
Previous work has linked self-efficacy to engagement in protective behaviours [7].
text.formatted: Previous work has linked self-efficacy to engagement in protective behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: However, results from the current study highlighted that while self-efficacy was associated with knowledge of ticks (i.e., people who were confident in tick removal had higher levels of knowledge), it was not associated with engagement in protective behaviours, meaning this confidence did not necessarily translate to real-world action.
In line with previous work [9], we found positive associations between engagement in protective behaviours and knowledge about ticks and TBDs and having seen or heard information about tick bites.
text.formatted: In line with previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>, we found positive associations between engagement in protective behaviours and knowledge about ticks and TBDs and having seen or heard information about tick bites.

text.text: While this suggests that knowledge may support behaviour, it is unlikely to be the only thing driving it.
Behaviour is multi-faceted, and numerous theories have highlighted that multiple factors are necessary for a behaviour to be enacted [10].
text.formatted: Behaviour is multi-faceted, and numerous theories have highlighted that multiple factors are necessary for a behaviour to be enacted <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: For example, previous work has highlighted that psychological factors including perceived likelihood of being bitten and lower levels of disgust were significant predictors of checking for ticks [7].
text.formatted: For example, previous work has highlighted that psychological factors including perceived likelihood of being bitten and lower levels of disgust were significant predictors of checking for ticks <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: It is also notable that in the current study, no variables independently predicted both knowledge and behaviour.

Work is needed to explore potential mechanisms of action, including the identification of barriers and facilitators to taking protective actions related to ticks to support engagement with these behaviours.
Some researchers have argued that a 'learning' effect takes place following tick encounters, where risk perceptions and engagement with tick checks are increased following experiences with ticks [9].
text.formatted: Some researchers have argued that a 'learning' effect takes place following tick encounters, where risk perceptions and engagement with tick checks are increased following experiences with ticks <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: While our study partially supports this, it is interesting that for protective behaviours, compared to those who had never been bitten by a tick, participants who thought that they had been bitten by a tick (but were not sure) had positive associations, unlike those who reported definitely being bitten by a tick.

This may suggest that perceived or suspected exposure to ticks, rather than confirmed experience, plays a role in motivations to engage in protective behaviours, potentially through altered perceptions of risk within these exposure groups.
While using an online survey allowed for the collection of data from participants across England, many participants provided 'don't know' responses.
Although this may reflect a lack of knowledge related to ticks, this could reflect limited engagement with survey items.

An additional limitation relates to the self-report nature of behavioural questions: previous research has demonstrated that the public can be confused about how to perform a tick check [7], with recent work highlighting that on average, only 42% of ticks in a simulated tick check were correctly identified by participants [11].
text.formatted: An additional limitation relates to the self-report nature of behavioural questions: previous research has demonstrated that the public can be confused about how to perform a tick check <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>, with recent work highlighting that on average, only 42% of ticks in a simulated tick check were correctly identified by participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: This may mean that responses provided by participants (i.e., 'I have performed a tick check') may not reflect optimal engagement in the specified protective behaviour.
Additionally, while region was included within the analysis, this was included at a broad geographical level.

Previous work has suggested that risk perceptions can differ for individuals in endemic areas [9], therefore, inclusion of more detailed geographical classifications within models may have provided additional insight related to the influence of local tick distribution and exposure risk.
text.formatted: Previous work has suggested that risk perceptions can differ for individuals in endemic areas <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>, therefore, inclusion of more detailed geographical classifications within models may have provided additional insight related to the influence of local tick distribution and exposure risk.

text.text: In conclusion, while sociodemographic factors were not consistently associated with knowledge of ticks or engagement in protective behaviours, several psychological variables were associated with these outcomes.
Although behaviour is unlikely to rely on one factor alone, these results also highlight the importance of knowledge in the engagement of protective behaviours.
Further work is needed to design and evaluate interventions aimed at increasing knowledge about ticks and TBDs.
